definition: A function f: K -> R on a finite CW complex (or simplicial complex) K assigning a real number to each cell, such that for each p-cell sigma: (1) at most one (p+1)-cell tau with sigma as a facet has f(tau) <= f(sigma), and (2) at most one (p-1)-face nu of sigma has f(nu) >= f(sigma). Introduced by Robin Forman (1998). A cell satisfying neither exception is critical.

contrasts.differential: Smooth Morse functions are on manifolds with non-degenerate critical points; discrete Morse functions are on cell/simplicial complexes with combinatorial critical cells
A discrete Morse function induces a discrete gradient vector field; conversely, any acyclic discrete vector field comes from a discrete Morse function

definition: A cell sigma in a discrete Morse function f is critical if it is unpaired: neither condition (1) nor (2) in the definition of discrete Morse function applies. Equivalently, sigma is not matched in the gradient vector field. Critical cells are the discrete analogue of critical points in smooth Morse theory. The Morse inequalities bound the number of critical p-cells below by the p-th Betti number.

contrasts.differential: A regular (non-critical) cell is paired with exactly one adjacent cell (either a facet or a cofacet) by the gradient vector field; a critical cell is unpaired
In smooth Morse theory, critical points are where the gradient vanishes; in discrete Morse theory, critical cells are unpaired cells in the gradient matching

definition: A discrete gradient vector field V on a CW complex K is a collection of pairs {(sigma^(p), tau^(p+1))} where sigma is a facet of tau, each cell appears in at most one pair, and there are no non-trivial closed V-paths (acyclicity). V is equivalent to an acyclic partial matching on the Hasse diagram of K. Unpaired cells are critical cells. Any acyclic discrete vector field is the gradient field of some discrete Morse function (Forman, 1998).

contrasts.differential: Smooth gradient fields are vector fields on manifolds derived from smooth functions; discrete gradient fields are matchings on cell complexes
A discrete vector field is any partial matching on the Hasse diagram; a gradient vector field additionally requires acyclicity (no closed V-paths)

definition: The discrete Morse inequalities relate critical cells to topology: (Weak) m_p >= b_p where m_p = number of critical p-cells and b_p = p-th Betti number. (Strong) sum_{i=0}^p (-1)^{p-i} m_i >= sum_{i=0}^p (-1)^{p-i} b_i for all p. These bound how few critical cells any discrete Morse function can have, generalizing the classical smooth Morse inequalities.

contrasts.differential: Betti numbers are topological invariants; the number of critical cells depends on the choice of Morse function but is always bounded below by the Betti numbers
A perfect discrete Morse function has m_p = b_p for all p (minimum possible critical cells). Not every complex admits a perfect Morse function

definition: An elementary collapse removes a free face pair (sigma, tau) where sigma is a facet of tau and sigma is a face of no other cell. This is a homotopy equivalence — the resulting complex has the same homotopy type as the original. A sequence of elementary collapses simplifies a complex while preserving its topology. Discrete Morse theory systematizes collapses: the regular cells define a sequence of elementary collapses, reducing to a complex built from critical cells only.

contrasts.differential: A collapse is a specific combinatorial operation on simplicial/CW complexes; a deformation retract is the continuous analogue. Collapses are deformation retracts but not conversely
The Morse complex is the result after all possible collapses — it consists only of critical cells and has the same homology as the original

definition: A V-path in a discrete gradient vector field V is an alternating sequence of cells sigma_0, tau_0, sigma_1, tau_1, ..., sigma_r where each (sigma_i, tau_i) is a pair in V and each sigma_{i+1} is a facet of tau_i distinct from sigma_i. The acyclicity condition requires no non-trivial closed V-paths. V-paths connect critical cells and define the boundary operator of the Morse complex.

contrasts.differential: In smooth Morse theory, flow lines are integral curves of the gradient field; V-paths are the discrete analogue, alternating between matched pairs
V-paths are combinatorial sequences on the complex; homotopies are continuous deformations. V-paths encode the combinatorial data needed to reconstruct the homotopy type

definition: For a discrete Morse function f: K -> R, the level set at value t is the subcomplex of cells with f-value <= t. As t increases, the level set grows by adding cells. When a regular pair is added, the homotopy type does not change. When a critical cell is added, the homotopy type changes exactly as in the smooth case: a critical p-cell either creates a new p-cycle or fills in a (p-1)-cycle.

contrasts.differential: In smooth Morse theory, level sets are preimages f^{-1}(t); in discrete Morse theory, they are subcomplexes of cells with f-value at most t
A filtration is a nested sequence of subcomplexes; the sublevel sets of a discrete Morse function form a specific filtration ordered by f-values

definition: In discrete Morse theory, the ascending manifold (or unstable manifold) of a critical cell sigma consists of all cells reachable from sigma by following V-paths in the gradient vector field upward (in the direction of increasing dimension). Together with descending manifolds, they provide a cell decomposition of the complex that reflects the topology encoded by the Morse function.

contrasts.differential: The ascending manifold follows V-paths upward from a critical cell; the descending manifold follows them downward. Their intersection pattern encodes the boundary operator of the Morse complex

definition: In discrete Morse theory, the descending manifold (or stable manifold) of a critical cell sigma consists of all cells from which sigma is reachable by following V-paths downward (in the direction of decreasing dimension). The descending manifolds of all critical cells partition the complex. In the smooth case, descending manifolds form the cells of a CW decomposition.

contrasts.differential: Descending manifold goes downward from a critical cell; ascending manifold goes upward. They are dual constructions
